A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PhysGaia, retaining the same 17 scenes and underlying simulation pipeline. The complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original monocular and multiview reconstruction experiments, per-scene results in Tables 9–10, and qualitative trajectory analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original dataset comparisons, quantitative trajectory evaluation, MoSca results, and physics-parameter estimation experiments.

M1.justification: The Houdini pipeline, FLIP/Pyro/MPM/Vellum solvers, and scene interaction procedures remain unchanged. The new Gaussian-splatting background, governing equations, and XPBD pseudocode expand documentation without establishing a changed generation algorithm or proposed reconstruction model. The new evaluation metrics are assessed under E3 and T1.

E1.justification: The same 17 scenes and monocular/multiview reconstruction tasks are retained. However, v2 actually evaluates Young’s modulus and Poisson’s ratio estimation on bouncing balls, previously discussed only as a potential application. It also empirically analyzes other physics and DyNVS datasets for motion complexity and visual distribution similarity, using TinyImageNet as the latter reference.

E2.justification: MoSca, previously only cited, joins the monocular quantitative and qualitative comparisons alongside D-3DGS, 4DGS, STG, and SoM. The new inverse-physics experiment evaluates PAC-NeRF and GIC, and trajectory evaluation includes a GT-GT oracle reference. The multiview reconstruction comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: Beyond the retained PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS evaluation, v2 introduces initial-frame trajectory matching, TD and cumulative-outlier AUOP evaluation, and an oracle control. It also adds Dynamic Score comparisons, FID/KID against TinyImageNet, and physics-parameter estimation evaluation. These substantially expand the evaluation design; existing camera configurations and image-quality protocols are retained.

E4.justification: v1’s physical-motion diagnosis relies on qualitative trajectory examples. v2 adds a low- versus high-dynamics comparison in Table 6, time-resolved outlier diagnostics in Figure 8, and a multi-object inverse-physics failure case in Section 5.3. Appendix E.2 also adds a dense-versus-sparse COLMAP depth-scaling observation.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new outlier percentages and oracle comparisons measure reconstruction errors and reference performance, rather than statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: All retained per-scene and aggregate image-quality scores are unchanged. v2 adds MoSca results, including monocular averages of 19.5 PSNR, 0.76 SSIM, and 0.34 LPIPS, plus dataset-comparison and trajectory scores. Table 7 newly reports Young’s modulus estimates of 1,700 for PAC-NeRF and 23,400 for GIC against ground truth of 100,000.

T1.justification: Section 4 introduces mathematical definitions for matched-trajectory TD and the persistent outlier process underlying AUOP, absent from v1. Appendix D additionally states constitutive assumptions, including linear elasticity and Kelvin–Voigt viscosity, and removes v1’s explicit non-Newtonian liquid qualification. These expand the formal specification; no new theorem or proof is presented.

C1.justification: The central claims about a diverse, physically simulated multi-body dataset with ground-truth trajectories and parameters remain stable. v2’s introduction explicitly adds novel evaluation metrics to the contribution, while its conclusion broadens the demonstrated applications from DyNVS evaluation to several tasks, including inverse physics.

C2.justification: v2 expands explanations of representation-specific reconstruction failures and interprets underestimated stiffness as excessive deformation used to fit multi-object observations. Appendix F replaces v1’s synthetic-to-real transfer discussion with limitations concerning constitutive simplifications, numerical discretization, and missing fine-scale dynamics. These materially revise both interpretation and applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: Appendix E newly identifies baseline configuration choices, public implementation links, training times, and a depth-scaling recommendation. Hardware reporting changes from four Titan Xp GPUs to one for simulation and from A6000 to A5000/A6000 for experiments. Most camera, rendering, and solver parameters are retained; these disclosures do not establish experimental reruns.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including FluidNexus, GIC, Vid2Sim, GP-4DGS, and evaluation-metric sources, and adds Phystwin to the dataset comparison table. Syn2Real disappears with the rewritten limitations discussion. The principal positioning against datasets with restricted materials, interactions, or physical ground truth remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The main narrative is extensively rewritten and reorganized. Dataset construction moves from the main text into expanded appendices, a metrics section takes its place, and empirical analysis is reorganized around benchmark comparison, reconstruction, and inverse physics. Terminology shifts from dataset toward benchmark and from viscoelastic toward rheological materials.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main layout, moves v1’s Figure 3 to the opening teaser, reorganizes material-result tables, and introduces colored rankings and MoSca columns. New motion-score and outlier plots accompany new evaluation tables. Existing scene and qualitative panels are extensively redistributed, including moves into the appendix.

improvement.justification: v1 provides physical ground truth but assesses reconstructed physical motion only qualitatively. v2’s explicit metrics, oracle-referenced trajectory results, and temporal error analysis substantially strengthen validation of the benchmark’s central purpose; the inverse-physics experiment also demonstrates a previously proposed application. Validation remains limited to two trajectory scenes, and the AUOP threshold is unspecified, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gain in empirical support.
